title: Expert defaults before calibration data
statement: When few students take each item, set item parameters from expert defaults and choose items by simple rules, because a statistically optimal method running on uncalibrated items does no better.
example: Calibrating one item takes at least 100 to 200 responses, which at about 10 students per course is 10 to 20 cohorts.
detail: The diagnostic guide in the reading project's knowledge base notes that estimating one item's difficulty and discrimination needs at least 100 to 200 responses, and slip and guess parameters typically 500 or more; with about 10 students in a course at a time, even 100 responses per item takes 10 to 20 cohorts, and revising an item resets the clock (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0154-diagnostic-assessment-brainlift.qmd`). It sets parameters from expert judgment and structural defaults instead, such as a guess rate of 0.25 for a four-option item and a slip rate of 0.10 to 0.15, and selects items by prerequisite structure, cluster sampling and sentinel items. On uncalibrated items, selection by expected information gain is no better than such rules and may be worse.
against: A later run found: A reading assessment's adaptive engine takes its uncalibrated difficulties from authoring bands, as this record advises, but picks each next item by information at the current estimate rather than by simple rules, following published adaptive-testing work; nothing in its package compares the two ways of selecting (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/01_PSYCHOMETRIC_DESIGN.md`).
